candidates.source_body_excerpt: Planners have given their blessing for the site of a former church to become homes. Zest Eco applied to Rochdale Council to build seven new houses on land at Egerton Street — the former New Jerusalem Church — in Middleton, which was founded before 1886 and was demolished by 2012. In planning documents, Zest said: “The proposal delivers seven three-bedroom family dwellings, each with private gardens and dedicated parking. “This form of development responds directly to the identified need for family housing rather than higher-density flat accommodation. “Full planning permission is sought for the erection of seven 2.5-storey three-bedroom townhouses with rear dormers, solar panels, associated parking, private gardens, landscaping and vehicular access via a new dropped kerb from Egerton Street. “The proposal regenerates a vacant brownfield site to deliver family housing within an established residential neighbourhood, respecting local character, safeguarding neighbouring amenity and providing safe and efficient access arrangements.” There were five objections to the plans, including a loss of on-street parking for existing residents, overdevelopment of the site and the loss of green space. candidates.source_summary: Oldham Athletic left to rue missing gilt-edged chances in derby defeat at Rochdale theoldhamtimes.co.uk
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Oldham Athletic suffered derby day defeat for the first time in a decade in the league. Latics looked comfortable in possession in the opening exchanges, albeit without doing anything to hurt Rochdale. But they were stung in the eighth minute when a cross from the right was flicked on in the box and Oldham looked to make amends from that early defensive lapse and carved out a number of openings. But they failed to capitalise on any of them. Just five minutes after falling behind Kane Drummond whipped a good ball into the box, Mike Fondop climbed to meet it but could not keep his free header down. Rochdale then struggled to deal with an Ollie Norburn corner that he sent to the far post, the ball was only half cleared but Gus Scott-Morriss' header was too tame to trouble goalkeeper Nils Ramming. But the worst of the misses came just before the half-hour. Keenan Appiah-Forson did well to put Ramming under pressure and force the keeper to lose control of the ball, it rolled for Fondop, but the striker put his low shot narrowly wide with an open goal at his mercy.

candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Rochdale lifted themselves off the foot of the League Two table with a 2-0 win against Oldham in their Greater Manchester derby.

The home side took the lead just seven minutes in. Charlie Tasker and Jonny Smith combined down the right, and Tasker's low delivery in behind the retreating Oldham defence was swept into the roof of the net by Dan Moss.

Oldham frontman Mike Fondop missed a gilt-edged chance on 25 minutes, sliding the ball wide of the post with an open goal at his mercy after a mistake from Dale stopper Nils Ramming, who had his pocket picked by Keenan Appiah-Forson.

The visitors continued to press forward after the interval, Kane Drummond's delivery across the face of goal eluding Fondop and substitute Calum Kavanagh.

Dale delivered a sucker punch when they doubled the lead on 62 minutes. Latics keeper Matt Hudson's kick towards the halfway line was met by Baba Adeeko, who headed the ball forward for Dajaune Brown to advance into the penalty area, side-step Donervon Daniels and slam a firm drive into the bottom corner.

candidates.source_title: Ian Watson praises Rochdale players after beating Oldham - East London and West Essex Guardian Series
candidates.source_summary: Ian Watson praises Rochdale players after beating Oldham East London and West Essex Guardian Series
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale boss Ian Watson praised his players for adapting to the demands of the Greater Manchester derby clash against Oldham following their 2-0 win at the Crown Oil Arena. Dan Moss’ seventh-minute opener eased the tension around the stadium, fans having called for Watson’s head in the previous home fixture, a 4-1 loss against Gillingham. Oldham spurned several chances before Dajaune Brown doubled the lead for Dale in the 62nd minute. The win lifted Watson’s men off the foot of the League Two table and secured bragging rights over their near neighbours. “Derby days bring a lot of tension and nerves and probably suit a different style than the one we like to play, these games are full of chaos,” said Watson. “But I thought we adapted and found a way to win the game incredibly well. Today was just about getting a result for the fans and for the club. The scoreboard was all that mattered. “The performance wasn’t where we want it to be, but derby days are almost an isolated case where you just need the scoreboard right and to get a good feeling around the club. “I’m incredibly proud of the boys. We’d spoken all week about what this game means to the fans and how much we wanted to run and duel with the opposition to show how much it means to us, and I thought the players did that.” In between Dale’s goals, Oldham had created several openings. Mike Fondop headed a good chance over and then fired wide with an open goal at his mercy after a mistake from Dale goalkeeper Nils Ramming. Oldham manager Micky Mellon was bitterly disappointed his side were unable to reward the travelling supporters and accepted responsibility for the result would fall on his shoulders.

Its promotional image generated by AI depicts large fairground rides, performers, balloons and crowds alongside a list of attractions including licensed bars, face painting, children's characters and games and information stalls.

Photos supplied from the venue on Saturday morning show around eight gazebos outside. The large fairground rides depicted in the promotional artwork are not visible in the photographs.

Those claims have not been independently verified; however, there have been multiple events captured by this page.

The same page published a warning on 9 September telling traders not to pay money upfront for stalls and made further allegations concerning previous events linked to Mr Boland.

A very similar event by the same organiser was forced to be cancelled by Salford City Council and GMP, the same 3-day event on 18, 19 and 20 August.

Those allegations have not been established as fact.

The photographs show activity taking place at The Pig and Whistle on Saturday but cannot establish everything available at the venue during the three-day event.

Resilient Roch is an innovative flood and climate resilience programme delivered through a partnership between Rochdale Borough Council and the National Flood Forum. Funded by the Flood and Coastal Innovation Programme (FCIP), the project seeks to improve resilience among households and communities vulnerable to flooding, particularly in disadvantaged and diverse neighbourhoods. Rather than relying on conventional consultation methods, Resilient Roch adopts a relationship-first approach that builds trust through long-term engagement with residents, community organisations, schools and local stakeholders. By integrating flood resilience with wider issues such as housing, health, wellbeing and climate awareness, the programme strengthens community preparedness and adaptation. Rochdale has a long history of flooding, including major events such as the 2015 Storm Eva floods, which affected hundreds of homes and businesses and exposed wider social vulnerabilities. Research highlighted that flood risk disproportionately affects disadvantaged communities, particularly where poor housing, low incomes, limited insurance uptake and institutional distrust intersect. Traditional engagement and consultation approaches often struggle to reach those most vulnerable to flooding, including marginalised communities, non-English speakers and socially isolated residents. The project aimed to increase flood and climate resilience across vulnerable communities while addressing barriers that limit participation. Key objectives included improving flood literacy, supporting the uptake of property flood resilience measures, strengthening financial resilience through insurance awareness, encouraging community ownership of flood preparedness and increasing understanding of climate risks. The programme also sought to develop stronger partnerships between residents, community organisations, local authorities and other stakeholders to create lasting resilience and community capacity. Resilient Roch adopted a place-based, relationship-led model of engagement that prioritised trust, local knowledge and long-term community presence. The project built on more than a decade of collaboration between Rochdale Borough Council and the National Flood Forum (NFF), enabling the programme to draw on established community trust, local knowledge and existing relationships rather than starting engagement from scratch.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Spectacular fire sculptures, lights and music will transform Rochdale Town Hall square this November A spectacular family festival will transform the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall this autumn. The Ignite Fire Festival is returning to the borough for three evenings of magical entertainment, complete with brand-new trails and attractions. Organised by Rochdale Development Agency, the free night-time event promises magical and immersive trails of fire, lights, and sound across Broadfield Slopes and the newly restored town hall grounds. The event runs from Friday, November 20 to Sunday, November 22, 2026, with the borough's official Christmas lights switch-on taking place on the Sunday evening. Last year, more than 10,000 people attended the festivities. Visitors will be able to walk through fiery displays, blazing sculptures, and an incredible illuminated installation created by multi-award-winning outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank. Community arts will also take centre stage, with a performance called 'Fireflies' featuring as part of the Culture Co-op programme. The showcase brings together Rochdale’s Skylight Circus Arts, interactive arts group Travelling Light Circus, and local residents who have trained specially to perform mesmerising fire-spinning feats. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “Ignite Fire Festival has been a huge hit with audiences across Greater Manchester and in just three years has grown to become one of the most popular events in the borough. This year, there will be really exciting new elements and attractions that will surprise, educate and entertain the whole family. Get the dates in your diary and look forward to the ultimate winter experience, and the perfect build-up to our Christmas lights switch-on.” The festival is funded by Rochdale Borough Council, Greater Manchester Combined Authority's Flexible Fund, and Rochdale Development Agency, in partnership with Walk the Plank and Culture Co-op. Further details will be released next month at rochdale.gov.uk/ignite .

candidates.source_title: Delivering for Rochdale, from our streets to the world stage - inyourarea.co.uk
candidates.source_summary: Delivering for Rochdale, from our streets to the world stage inyourarea.co.uk
candidates.source_body_excerpt: When I was a lad growing up on a council estate in Spotland, the idea that a Rochdale MP might one day sit round a table in government would have seemed far-fetched. For nearly two hundred years this town sent its members to Parliament without a single one of them holding a departmental ministerial post. That changed this summer, and I still feel the weight of it. Being appointed Minister for Early Education by Prime Minister Andy Burnham is the honour of my working life. But a title only matters if it delivers something real for the people back home. So this month I want to tell you what that job has actually meant for Rochdale. Much of my brief is about giving children the best possible start in life, and over the holidays I saw exactly what that looks like on the ground. At KYP, at BACP, at Aspire 2 Inspire in Greenbank, and with the Rochdale Nigerian Community Association in Broadfield Park, I watched local youngsters get a proper meal and a day full of sport, science and fun through the Government's Holiday Activities and Food programme. As the minister now responsible for that programme across the whole country, there is a real pride in seeing our own community groups make it work so well right here. I also visited the Best Start Family Hub on Derby Street in Heywood, one of seventeen hubs across our borough that support families from bump and birth through those crucial early years. That support makes a real difference to families across our borough, and I will fight to expand it. None of this is charity. It is the difference a Government makes when it decides that where you are born should never decide how far you get. That same principle runs through the £20m of Pride in Place money coming to Smallbridge, Hurstead and Belfield over the next ten years. This is your money to shape, so I have been out and about hearing what local people actually want from it, from Haroon's chippy on Stevenson Square to the team at Cohen's Chemist. The whole point of this fund is to give local people a real say, and I intend to make sure that promise is kept. Ministerial red boxes have not kept me away from the things that make our town what it is. Over the past few weeks I have cheered on the Hornets, welcomed the veterans of Get Together After Serving as they opened their brilliant new cafe opposite Rochdale AFC, joined the Armed Forces Breakfast Club at the Flying Horse for Parachute Regiment veteran Brian Lamb's 90th birthday, and stood in a packed Town Hall Square as OMD paid tribute to the town where they began. Rochdale at its very best. This week my work takes me a good deal further afield. I am in Paris representing the United Kingdom at UNESCO's Digital Learning Week, where education ministers from more than twenty-five countries are wrestling with one of the biggest questions of our age: how we make the most of artificial intelligence in our classrooms without losing what makes teaching human.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Find out the latest events from September 19 from All Across the Arts columnist Steve Cooke The Octagon’s 30th anniversary production of East is East, Ayub Khan Din’s thoughtful comedy of life in a Pakistani/English family in early 1970s Salford is an engaging homage to this modern classic. It works extremely well in the Octagon’s intimate space with Rachana Jadhav’s big, impressive set spreading across about a third of the auditorium. The three main acting areas encompass a central one that transforms from the Khan family’s kitchen to their business - a fish and chip shop, and briefly to their front parlour; another to represent their back yard, complete with the “shed” that bundle of nervous energy, youngster Sajit retreats to and “sunbathes” on top of in his protective but rather smelly parka. and another, representing the base of a factory chimney, with a balustrade where the brothers can be together, away from mum and dad. The transformations are done entertainingly by the cast with music and dancing, Jane Lalljee’s lighting very effectively enhancing changes of locale. Director Kash Arshad summarises the plot as being “the experience of being brought up in a Muslim household, with a white British mother and a Pakistani father, who ran his own business, with kids who felt not British enough to be British nor Pakistani enough to be Pakistani.” Overbearing with self-importance dad George Khan is trying to rule his family for what he believes is the best according to religion and tradition. The breaking point comes when he attempts to make arranged marriages for two of his sons who see the world in very different ways.

Last night, Middleton Township Committee approved a traffic order which will introduce three pedestrian crossing islands, extend bus stops, reduce on-street parking and narrow parts of Grimshaw Lane following problems with speeding, serious crashes, including a fatality, and inconsiderate parking blocking buses. The scheme was called in to be considered by the committee following objections from 11 residents, with the main concern being the loss of parking outside homes. The road is very dangerous. There have been multiple RTAs, parked cars crashed into, property damaged repeatedly and a fatality. “The road layout was identified as a major factor in the number of accidents and this scheme addresses this. “The islands narrow the road and force the cars to slow down. The narrowing of junctions with disabled access crossings include Shawbury Street, Sedgley Street and the two Sandy Lanes. “We carried out extensive consultation on this scheme. candidates.source_summary: The New York State Comptroller’s Office says it is planning on starting an audit of the finances of Rochdale Village, at the urging of local elected officials.“I am writing to
candidates.source_body_excerpt: State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli, inset, has agreed to start an audit of Rochdale Village, after a carrying charge spike last year. The New York State Comptroller’s Office says it is planning on starting an audit of the finances of Rochdale Village, at the urging of local elected officials. “I am writing to let you know that we have formally engaged the audit of Roachdale Village Inc.’s finances,” wrote Comptroller Tom DiNapoli in a letter dated Aug. 25 and addressed to the city councilman, Ty Hankerson (D-Jamaica), as well as the area’s state reps: Assemblymembers Vivian Cook (D-Jamaica) and Khaleel Anderson (D-South Ozone Park), and Sens. Leroy Comrie (D-St. Albans) and James Sanders Jr. (D-South Ozone Park). Hankerson posted the letter on his Instagram page on Sept. 8 and wrote, in the caption, “ROCHDALE, I’ve got good news! The audit is coming and DHCR has officially been engaged for the reassessment of carrying charges,” he wrote, in reference to the Division of Housing and Community Renewal, the state agency that oversees the financially troubled Mitchell-Lama co-op, home to 25,000 people, and hit with $17.7 million in past-due water bills, along with interest. “We’ve been working really, really hard on this,” Hankerson told the Chronicle in an interview. In early August, Hankerson penned a letter addressed to DiNapoli requesting “a full audit” of the co-op’s finances, and a recalculation of the carrying charges that its members are paying in lieu of rent. “Residents should not be asked to carry costs that have not been fully reviewed, explained, and justified,” Hankerson wrote at the time. Last year, the DHCR increased carrying charges at the complex by more than 20 percent, leading to protests.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: The new site is planned for moorland between Rochdale and Rossendale, next to the existing Scout Moor wind farm Developers have cut the number of turbines proposed for a major wind farm on moorland after reviewing feedback from residents and organisations. Renewable energy firm Cubico Sustainable Investments has reduced the number of proposed turbines at Scout Moor II, between Rochdale and Rossendale, from 17 to 12. The site would be next to the existing Scout Moor wind farm. The revised plans have been submitted to Rochdale and Rossendale councils and will now be subject to a further round of consultation before councillors whether to approve it. Campaign group Friends of the Moorland said it was unlikely the revisions would address all of its concerns. Steve Davison from the group said: "We need to review the plans in detail to come to a considered view but it's unlikely that all of our fundamental objections will have been addressed." Each turbine could be up to 590ft (180m) tall, making them taller than Blackpool Tower. The proposals previously prompted hundreds of objections and opponents warned of the impact on peatland, wildlife and the landscape.

candidates.source_title: Hat trick of announcements as Middleton’s regeneration moves up a gear – Rochdale Borough Council
candidates.source_summary: A hat trick of announcements has cemented Middleton’s renewed regeneration drive, as its Mayoral Development Corporation continues to take shape.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A hat trick of announcements has cemented Middleton’s renewed regeneration drive, as its Mayoral Development Corporation continues to take shape. Among them is news that the Middleton Old Grammar School, recently bought by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. Founded in 1582, the building in Boarshaw Road aimed to provide free education to children in the parish of Middleton. More recently, it was used as a wedding and events venue before the council took the opportunity to buy the heritage asset when it went up for sale. A feasibility study is now on going, with a view to the building being repaired, refurbished and reopened for community use in the future. The news was announced at an event at Middleton Arena to update residents and businesses about the results of an engagement exercise titled, ‘Our Town, Our Future’ and on going work to create a Mayoral Development Corporation to further drive regeneration in the town. Chaired by the proposed chairs of Middleton’s MDC, Steve Coogan and Rose Marley, and attended by Mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, and Rochdale Borough Council leader, Councillor Neil Emmott, the event attracted more than 500 residents and local business leaders. The announcements followed news that the council is in the process of acquiring long derelict Warwick Mill and neighbouring 1960s office block, London House, with a view to bringing the mill back into use, possibly as new homes, and demolishing London House. In a further boost, attendees also learned that the Middleton Scout Hut will be repurposed as a community venue, with a full programme of activities and training opportunities for young people. The council owned venue on Long Street has been vacant for 13 years and the council has now agreed a long-term lease with charitable organisation, the Groundwork Trust. Proposals for the building include the creation of a hub for workshops to teach ecology and construction skills. The building will also serve as a base for local environmental projects, and, while opportunities for young people will be a key focus, it will also be a space for community groups to get together to help tackle social isolation.

The warning comes after only half of last year’s late applicants (51%) were offered a place at their first-choice school, compared with 87% of those who applied on time. While Rochdale Council says there is no guarantee that any applicant will be offered a place at their preferred secondary school and a number of other factors are taken into account, completing an application on time is an important part of the admissions process. This is because late applications are not processed until after National Offer Day (March 1, 2027), the day when families discover which school their child will attend. Schools do not reserve places for late applications, meaning they may already be full before a late application is considered. Cllr Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, said: “Choosing the right secondary school for a child is one of the most important decisions families make and it’s not something to be left until the last minute. “As a parent who has gone through the process already, I know how much thought goes into making these preferences as ultimately this is the school that will shape your child’s educational journey and where they will sit their GCSEs. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Residents have launched a petition to replace a popular kick pitch which is being turned into a car park. Campaigners say the pitch in Burnside Crescent in Langley, Middleton, has been a community hub, as well as somewhere people can enjoy kicking around a football and enjoying other sports. The pitch is one of three on the estate. It is managed by the Burnside Centre and is being turned into a car park for the centre following planning permission for change of use. Families say they have been told a replacement will be created further away at Rochdale AFC and Rochdale Council’s planned Football and Community Wellbeing Hub at Bowlee Playing Fields. Instead, they are calling for a new pitch to be created on land next to the original. Launching the petition on Change.org, Kelly Burton shared: “For countless children and teenagers in the Burnside Crescent area, the kick pitch behind the old site was more than just a recreational space — it was a community hub where friendships were formed and cherished memories were built. “Every day, hundreds of young players gathered there, practicing their football skills, learning the value of teamwork, and enjoying the joy of outdoor play. “Recently, the kick pitch was removed without prior notice to the public. This decision has left a significant void in our community, with children now deprived of a convenient, safe, and free space to play.
